chunks: "I2C stands for Inter-Integrated Circuit, usually pronounced 'I squared C'.
It's a two-wire serial bus that Philips, now NXP, created in the early 1980 seconds so that chips inside the same product could talk without needing many pins.
The two wires are SCL, the clock, and SDA, the data. Both are open-drain: any device can pull a line low, but nobody drives it high; a pull-up resistor does that.
Because of this, many devices can share the same two wires without damaging each other. Every device on the bus has an address, usually 7 bits.
A controller, which used to be called the master, starts a transaction with a START condition, sends the address plus a read-write bit, and the device with that address answers with an ACK.
Then bytes flow, each followed by an ACK bit, until the controller sends a STOP.

It's slow, 100 kilohertz standard, 400 kilohertz fast, 1 megahertz fast-mode plus, but it's perfect for things like temperature sensors, EEPROMs, real-time clocks, power management chips, where you want lots of devices on very few pins.
And it supports multiple controllers with arbitration, plus clock stretching, so a slow device can pause the clock."
